To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we determined the conformation and orientation of the pore-former TatA in the lipid membrane, which will help to understand its mechanism of transport.
the transmembrane and amphiphilic parts of the pore-former of the twin-argine translocase are α-helical and that the amphiphile is tilted with respect to the membrane normal.

the membrane-bound TatA(d) is a two-helix protein, the transmembrane and the amphiphillic helices are tilted by 13° and 64°, respectively, the latter helix is rotated by 235° around the helix axis with respect to the transmembraneous helix and that the amphiphile region is not flexible but rather forms an integral part of the protein structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a new class of membrane proteins and provides the first structural insights into the membrane topology of TatA, which are important for a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms of protein translocation.
the membrane insertion of TatA(d) in the lipid environment of the native membrane.
the structure of a protein in its natural environment, the membrane.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the membrane-bound state of TatA(d) is a well-defined, stable structure that is different from the structure in micelles.
the TatA(2, 3, 4, 5, 7) helices form an antiparallel β-sheet, with the APHs of the monomers forming a β-hairpin that is stabilized by salt bridges.
the transmembrane domain of TatA(d) is tilted in the membrane and that the amphiphatic helix is tilted and rotated relative to the transmembranous helix.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure of TatA(d) in the membrane-bound form is similar to its structure in detergent micelles but that the amphiphile is not aligned in the same way in the two environments.
the membrane-bound state of TatA(d) is characterized by a transmembrane α-helix and a slanted amphiphilic α-helix that are both aligned with the membrane surface.
we have resolved the membrane alignment of TatA in a membrane mimetic system and have shown that the amphiphatic helix of TatA(d) is slanted in the membrane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
solid-state NMR is an extremely powerful tool for the determination of membrane protein structures.

solid-state NMR is a powerful tool to determine the conformation of membrane-bound proteins in their native membrane environment and can be used to resolve ambiguities arising from other biophysical techniques.
a combination of liquid- and solid-state NMR experiments is required for the complete structural characterization of TatA in its membrane-embedded state.
